title: Pauli errors and the repetition code
summary: Store a qubit in three, measure parities through ancillas, and correct a bit flip without learning the state.
why: Every resource estimate rests on this mechanism: parity checks locate errors without measuring the data, and distance sets how fast failures fall.
advantage: Not a speedup: error correction is the overhead that makes long quantum computations possible at all.

title: Stabilizers, tableaus and Gottesman–Knill
summary: Describe states by the Pauli strings that leave them unchanged, and simulate Clifford circuits efficiently.
why: Error-correction circuits are Clifford circuits with Pauli noise, so they can be simulated at scale; non-Clifford gates are what make fault-tolerant computation expensive.
advantage: Efficient classical simulation of a restricted circuit family; it marks where quantum advantage cannot come from.

title: The surface code at distance 3
summary: Seventeen qubits, eight local checks, one logical qubit: the code current hardware uses.
why: Its 2d²−1 qubits per logical qubit is the multiplier that turns logical-qubit counts into physical-qubit counts.
advantage: Not a speedup: a local code with a threshold, at quadratic qubit cost in the distance.

title: Noise models, thresholds and the suppression factor Λ
summary: Predict logical error per cycle from physical noise, and size the code distance for a target, using Google's 2024 data.
why: Λ and the target error per cycle decide the code distance, and with it most of a machine's physical-qubit count.
advantage: Not a speedup: the scaling law that converts error rates into qubit overhead.

title: Decoding I: detection events and minimum-weight matching
summary: Turn noisy syndrome history into a correction by matching detection events on a weighted graph.
why: The decoder is classical infrastructure that must run continuously and fast; its accuracy is part of Λ and its speed bounds the logical clock.
advantage: Polynomial-time classical decoding; exact matching here is exponential and for teaching only.

title: Decoding II: union-find and the accuracy–speed trade-off
summary: Grow clusters around defects by half-edges, merge them with a union-find structure, then peel a correction, trading a little accuracy for almost-linear worst-case time.
why: The decoder's worst-case time sets the logical clock and its accuracy sets the code distance, so choosing a decoder is a cost decision in the qubit and infrastructure budget.
advantage: Worst case O(n α(n)), with simulated toric-code thresholds slightly below matching (9.9% vs 10.3%); the repository's version is written for clarity and does not reach that bound.

title: Real-time decoding: throughput, backlog and latency
summary: Size the syndrome stream, show why a decoder slower than it causes Terhal's exponential backlog under T-gate feedforward, and see how windowed parallel decoding and dedicated hardware address throughput and latency.
why: Decoder throughput, latency, bandwidth and power are where classical infrastructure becomes the binding constraint on fault-tolerant runtime.
advantage: No quantum-advantage claim: decoder throughput must exceed the generation rate (f < 1, with margin) to avoid exponential slowdown.

title: Logical operations: lattice surgery, cheap Cliffords and expensive T gates
summary: Logical Paulis become classical frame updates, Clifford gates come from lattice-surgery joint measurements, and a T gate consumes a magic state with a correction that depends on the measurement outcome.
why: This is why resource estimates count T or Toffoli gates and why decoder reaction time is on the critical path.
advantage: Not a speedup. It sets the cost tiers (free Paulis, about d cycles per Clifford, distilled and latency-bound T gates) that every runtime estimate uses.

title: Magic states: distillation, cultivation and the logical clock
summary: 15-to-1 distillation cubes the magic-state error, factories cost qubits and cycles, and the machine runs at the lower of the factory T-rate and one dependent T gate per reaction time.
why: It turns a T or Toffoli count into wall-clock time and factory qubits, and shows where decoder latency becomes the binding constraint.
advantage: Not a speedup. It sets the logical clock speed and the magic-state footprint that decide fault-tolerant runtime.

title: The control and calibration stack
summary: The per-qubit lines, cryostat heat and space limits, and calibration as a dependency graph that a surface code needs on transmon hardware.
why: It shows where infrastructure (wiring, electronics, data rates, calibration orchestration) limits scaling before the physics does.
advantage: Not a speedup: this is the engineering cost any fault-tolerant advantage must carry.

title: End-to-end resource estimation
summary: From logical qubits and Toffoli counts to code distance, physical qubits and runtime, reproducing two 2021 published estimates; the simple model does not capture the newest (2025) architectures.
why: This is the calculation a business decision rests on: it shows which hardware assumptions drive the qubit count and the runtime.
advantage: Not a speedup: the accounting that decides whether an algorithmic speedup survives error-correction overhead.

title: Hardware modalities and roadmaps
summary: Superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, cat (bosonic), photonic and topological qubits compared by cycle time, connectivity and errors, with every roadmap item a dated claim.
why: It turns vendor roadmaps into checkable inputs (cycle time, reaction time, code) for the resource model behind a timing decision.
advantage: Not a speedup: slower reaction times scale wall-clock time linearly; connectivity reduces qubit counts, not dependent-step latency.

title: The full chain: from application to timeline
summary: Run one workload from application to hardware, and separate what binds today (Λ, device physics) from what binds once Λ ≈ 10 (decoding, control, calibration).
why: The decision path's conclusion: a list of checkable conditions in place of a single qubit count or date.
advantage: Synthesis: no new speedup; it shows which conditions an advantage claim depends on.
